cyber_essentials.title: Cyber Essentials
cyber_essentials.intro: Ten scenario questions covering the five Cyber Essentials technical controls — Firewalls, Secure Configuration, Security Update Management, User Access Control and Malware Protection. Sourced directly from NCSC's own “Cyber Essentials: Requirements for IT Infrastructure v3.3” (Crown Copyright).

questions.scenario: Your IT contractor sets up remote access to your office firewall's admin interface so they can manage it from home — using the firewall's factory default admin password, since nobody's got round to changing it.
questions.question: Which Cyber Essentials requirement does this breach?
options: Nothing — factory passwords are fine as long as the interface isn't advertised publicly
Default admin passwords must be changed to a strong, unique password — or remote admin access disabled entirely
Firewalls only need protecting if the office uses public wifi
Only cloud firewalls require a password change
questions.explanation: For every firewall, you must change default administrative passwords to a strong and unique password — or disable remote administrative access entirely. Internet-facing admin interfaces additionally need MFA or an IP allow list.
questions.why: The admin interface is the master control for everything the firewall protects — if an attacker can log into it, every other firewall rule stops mattering, because they can simply reconfigure or switch off the protection itself. A factory default password is public information (it's in the manual), so leaving it unchanged is functionally the same as leaving the front door key under the mat with a sign pointing to it.
questions.reference: Cyber Essentials: Requirements for IT Infrastructure v3.3 — Section E.1, Firewalls

questions.scenario: A new starter's laptop is connected straight to the office network before IT has applied any configuration at all.
questions.question: What must the firewall do by default with any inbound connection that hasn't been explicitly allowed?
options: Allow it through, then log it for review later
Block unauthenticated inbound connections by default
Only block it if the source is outside the UK
Ask the user to confirm by email first
questions.explanation: Cyber Essentials requires that unauthenticated inbound connections are blocked by default — nothing gets in unless a documented, approved firewall rule lets it.
questions.why: Every internet-connected device is constantly scanned by automated tools looking for anything that responds — this starts within minutes of a device going online, not just when someone specifically targets your business. Blocking unrequested inbound traffic by default means an unconfigured device presents nothing to find, rather than quietly waiting to be discovered by whatever's scanning that day.
questions.reference: Cyber Essentials: Requirements for IT Infrastructure v3.3 — Section E.1, Firewalls

questions.scenario: A shared team laptop is set to auto-login with no PIN or password, so nobody has to type anything to start using it each morning.
questions.question: Does this meet Cyber Essentials' secure configuration requirements?
options: Yes — convenience is fine as long as the office itself is locked
No — a credential (biometric, password or PIN) must be required before a user can access a device's services
Yes, but only laptops are exempt from this rule
Only an issue if the laptop ever leaves the building
questions.explanation: If a device requires a user's physical presence to access it, a credential must be in place before access is granted — and that credential must be protected against brute-force guessing (throttling or a lockout after no more than 10 attempts).
questions.why: A device with no credential gives away everything the moment it's physically accessible — a lost laptop on a train, an unattended desk, a stolen phone — no hacking skill required, just proximity. The brute-force protections matter too: without a throttle or lockout, even a real credential can eventually be guessed by a program trying thousands of combinations automatically, so the credential alone isn't the whole story.
questions.reference: Cyber Essentials: Requirements for IT Infrastructure v3.3 — Section E.2, Secure Configuration (Device unlocking credentials)

questions.scenario: A server set up three years ago still has its original built-in “Guest” account enabled, unused, with its default password never changed.
questions.question: What does Cyber Essentials require here?
options: Nothing — an unused account isn't a real risk
Remove or disable unnecessary user accounts, such as unused guest and administrative accounts, and change any default or guessable passwords
Only relevant if the server is directly internet-facing
Rename the account rather than remove it
questions.explanation: Organisations must regularly remove or disable unnecessary user accounts and change any default or guessable account passwords — an unused account with a default password is exactly the kind of weak point Secure Configuration exists to close.
questions.why: Every account, used or not, is a potential way in — and an old Guest account nobody remembers is worse than a well-known one, because nobody's watching for it being used. Default installs create these weak points automatically (pre-set passwords, spare accounts, unnecessary services quietly running), which is exactly why Secure Configuration exists as its own control rather than being assumed covered by the other four.
questions.reference: Cyber Essentials: Requirements for IT Infrastructure v3.3 — Section E.2, Secure Configuration

questions.scenario: A vendor releases a patch rated “critical” for software your business relies on. Three weeks later, it still hasn't been applied.
questions.question: Does this meet the requirement?
options: Yes, as long as it's applied within 30 days
No — critical or high-risk updates (CVSS v3 score 7 or above) must be applied within 14 days of release
Yes — updates are only mandatory for servers
It depends on whether the vendor sent a reminder email
questions.explanation: Updates that fix vulnerabilities described as ‘critical’ or ‘high risk’ (or scoring 7+ on CVSS v3) must be applied within 14 days of release — three weeks is outside that window.
questions.why: Publishing a security patch effectively announces where a weakness was — attackers study updates specifically to work out what they fix, then go looking for anyone who hasn't applied it yet. The 14-day window isn't arbitrary caution, it's a race against exactly that process, and three weeks gives real attackers a real head start on a known, public weakness.
questions.reference: Cyber Essentials: Requirements for IT Infrastructure v3.3 — Section E.3, Security Update Management

questions.scenario: Your business still runs an accounting package the vendor stopped supporting — and stopped issuing security fixes for — two years ago. It still works fine day to day.
questions.question: What does Cyber Essentials require?
options: Keep using it as long as it hasn't been compromised yet
It must be removed from in-scope devices, or removed from scope entirely via a defined sub-set with no internet traffic
Only a problem if it's a Windows application
Fine as long as a firewall is in place in front of it
questions.explanation: All software on in-scope devices must be licensed and supported, and removed from devices once it becomes unsupported (or excluded from scope via a properly defined, internet-isolated sub-set).
questions.why: Once a vendor stops supporting a product, any new vulnerability discovered in it will never get fixed — the gap between what's protected and what's exploitable only grows over time, with no way to close it while the software stays connected to your network. "It still works fine" describes functionality, not security — the two aren't the same thing, and unsupported software is a permanently open door, not a currently-quiet one.
questions.reference: Cyber Essentials: Requirements for IT Infrastructure v3.3 — Section E.3, Security Update Management

questions.scenario: Jody, an IT administrator, uses their admin account for everyday email and web browsing, not just for admin tasks.
questions.question: Why does Cyber Essentials treat this as a risk, and what's required instead?
options: It's fine — administrators are trusted users
Separate accounts must be used for administrative activities only — malware opened via email or a browser inherits whatever privilege level the account has
It's only a problem if Jody shares the password with anyone
Only domain administrator accounts are covered by this rule, not local ones
questions.explanation: Organisations must use separate accounts for administrative activities only, with no emailing, web browsing or other standard activity that could expose admin privileges to avoidable risk — if malware runs under an admin account, it acquires admin-level access too.
questions.why: This is the actual mechanism, not just a rule for its own sake: if malware reaches a device through an email or a browser, it runs with whatever privileges the logged-in account already has. On a standard account, the damage is limited. On an admin account, the same malware can rewrite system files, create new accounts, and spread much further. NCSC's own guidance describes exactly this scenario — an admin account opening a malicious attachment let ransomware encrypt far more of the network than a standard account ever could have reached, purely because of which account happened to be logged in when the click happened.
questions.reference: Cyber Essentials: Requirements for IT Infrastructure v3.3 — Section E.4, User Access Control

questions.scenario: Your business uses a cloud accounting platform. Staff log in with just a username and password — no second factor.
questions.question: Does this meet Cyber Essentials?
options: Yes, as long as the password is 12+ characters
No — authentication to cloud services must always use multi-factor authentication
Only the admin account needs MFA
Only required if the platform stores payment data
questions.explanation: Cyber Essentials requires MFA wherever available — and authentication to cloud services must always use MFA, regardless of password length.
questions.why: A password on its own is only as strong as the last place someone reused it — password lists leaked from unrelated websites get tried against completely different services, and it works often enough to be worth an attacker's time. MFA means a stolen password alone isn't enough to get in, which matters especially for cloud services since, unlike an office network, they're reachable by anyone on the internet, not just someone already inside your building.
questions.reference: Cyber Essentials: Requirements for IT Infrastructure v3.3 — Section E.4, User Access Control (Multi-factor authentication)

questions.scenario: You issue locked-down tablets to field staff that can only run apps from an approved, code-signed list — no anti-malware software is installed.
questions.question: Does this satisfy the malware protection control?
options: No — anti-malware software is always mandatory regardless of other controls
Yes — application allow listing (approved, code-signed apps only) is a valid alternative to anti-malware software
Only acceptable for mobile phones, not tablets
Only if it's also combined with a firewall
questions.explanation: For any in-scope device, you need at least one of: anti-malware software, or application allow listing — approved, code-signed applications only, with an actively maintained approval list. Both are valid, not just anti-malware.
questions.why: Traditional anti-malware works by recognising threats it already knows about — which means brand-new malware nobody's seen before can slip through until a vendor catches up and issues a detection for it. Allow listing flips that model entirely: nothing runs unless it's already approved, so it doesn't matter whether something is old or brand new — if it's not on the list, it simply never gets the chance to execute in the first place.
questions.reference: Cyber Essentials: Requirements for IT Infrastructure v3.3 — Section E.5, Malware Protection (Application allow listing)

questions.scenario: Your Windows laptops have Microsoft Defender running, but nobody's checked whether it's actually configured correctly or being kept up to date.
questions.question: Is “it's installed” enough to meet the requirement?
options: Yes — the presence of any anti-malware tool is sufficient
No — it must be active, kept up to date per the vendor's instructions, and configured to prevent malware running, block malicious code execution, and block connections to malicious websites
Only needs checking once a year
Only matters for servers, not laptops
questions.explanation: Anti-malware software must be updated in line with vendor recommendations and configured to prevent malware running, prevent execution of malicious code, and prevent connections to malicious websites — installed-but-unconfigured doesn't meet the bar.
questions.why: An anti-malware tool that's installed but not actively maintained only protects against what existed at install time — new malware appears constantly, so real protection quietly decays day by day even though the icon in the taskbar looks exactly the same as it always did. "Installed" creates a false sense of security; "active and kept current" is what the requirement is actually asking for, because that's the only version of it that still works.
questions.reference: Cyber Essentials: Requirements for IT Infrastructure v3.3 — Section E.5, Malware Protection (Anti-malware software)

gdpr.title: GDPR
gdpr.intro: Ten scenario questions covering the UK GDPR principles and individual rights that come up most in day-to-day supplier operations — lawfulness and consent, data minimisation and retention, security, breach reporting, subject access, erasure, controllers vs processors, and special category data. Sourced directly from the ICO's own guidance.

questions.scenario: A company starts emailing marketing offers to everyone on its supplier contact list, using addresses that were only ever given for invoicing purposes — without telling anyone or checking whether it's allowed.
questions.question: Does this meet the UK GDPR's first principle?
options: Yes — business marketing is always a reasonable use of contact data
No — you must identify a valid lawful basis for this specific use, and be clear and open about it, before processing data this way
Yes, as long as an unsubscribe link is included
Only a problem if someone actually complains
questions.explanation: You must identify valid grounds (a “lawful basis”) under the UK GDPR for collecting and using personal data, and be clear, open and honest with people from the start about how you'll use it. Using invoicing contacts for marketing, with no lawful basis and no transparency, breaches this principle.
questions.why: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency comes first among the UK GDPR's seven principles because everything else depends on it — no amount of good security or accurate record-keeping fixes the fact that you never had a valid reason to process the data in the first place. Using data for a new purpose people weren't told about also breaks their reasonable expectations, which is exactly what “fairness” exists to protect.
questions.reference: ICO Guide to the UK GDPR — Principle (a): Lawfulness, Fairness and Transparency

questions.scenario: A website's newsletter sign-up box is pre-ticked by default, so visitors have to actively un-tick it to avoid being added to the mailing list.
questions.question: Does this meet the UK GDPR's standard for consent?
options: Yes, as long as there's a way to opt out later
No — consent requires a positive opt-in; pre-ticked boxes or any other method of default consent don't meet the standard
Yes, pre-ticking is an accepted shortcut for newsletters specifically
Only an issue for special category data
questions.explanation: Consent requires a positive opt-in — organisations must not use pre-ticked boxes or any other method of default consent. Genuine consent has to be freely given, specific, and an active choice, not something people have to notice and undo.
questions.why: The whole point of consent as a lawful basis is giving people real control — a pre-ticked box quietly assumes agreement nobody actually gave, which defeats that purpose entirely. It's also one of the most commonly cited failures in real ICO enforcement action, precisely because it looks compliant at a glance while not actually being a choice at all.
questions.reference: ICO Guidance on Consent

questions.scenario: An online job application form asks every applicant for their date of birth, marital status and religion “just in case it's useful later,” even though none of it is relevant to the role being advertised.
questions.question: Does this meet the data minimisation principle?
options: Yes — collecting more data upfront saves having to ask again later
No — personal data must be adequate, relevant, and limited to what's necessary for the stated purpose; “might be useful” isn't the same as “necessary”
Yes, as long as the form marks the fields as optional
Only a problem if the data is later shared with someone else
questions.explanation: Personal data must be adequate, relevant, and limited to what is necessary for your specified purpose — collecting sensitive data “just in case” fails all three tests at once.
questions.why: Every extra piece of data held is something that now has to be secured, justified and eventually deleted — data minimisation isn't just a paperwork exercise, it directly shrinks the damage a future breach could do, since nothing can leak that was never collected. Religion in particular is “special category data” under Article 9, which needs its own separate legal justification most job application forms don't have.
questions.reference: ICO Guide to the UK GDPR — Principle (c): Data Minimisation

questions.scenario: A company still holds full CVs and application details for every candidate who's applied for a job in the last eight years — including people never hired — with no policy on when any of it gets deleted.
questions.question: Does this meet the storage limitation principle?
options: Yes, as long as the data is kept securely
No — personal data must not be kept longer than needed, and organisations need a retention policy with regular review and deletion
Yes — keeping records indefinitely protects against future legal claims
Only relevant for customer data, not job applicants
questions.explanation: You must not keep personal data for longer than you need it, and should have a policy setting standard retention periods, reviewing what's held, and erasing or anonymising it once it's no longer needed.
questions.why: Data doesn't get safer the longer it's kept — it becomes a bigger, staler liability, fully exposed in any future breach but with less and less legitimate purpose behind holding it. Unsuccessful job applicants in particular have a reasonable expectation their details won't sit on file indefinitely once a role's been filled — “might need it someday” isn't a retention policy.
questions.reference: ICO Guide to the UK GDPR — Principle (e): Storage Limitation

questions.scenario: A company emails a spreadsheet of customer names, addresses and order histories to a subcontractor, unencrypted, over regular email.
questions.question: Does this meet the UK GDPR's security principle?
options: Yes — email is a normal, everyday business tool
No — appropriate technical and organisational measures (such as encryption where appropriate) are required to protect personal data's confidentiality, integrity and availability
Yes, as long as the subcontractor has signed a contract
Only relevant for special category data
questions.explanation: The security principle requires “appropriate technical and organisational measures” to protect personal data — including encryption and pseudonymisation where appropriate, proportionate to the risk the processing poses.
questions.why: An unencrypted email can be intercepted, misaddressed, or sit unsecured in an inbox indefinitely — “appropriate” measures are judged against exactly that kind of realistic risk, not just whether the tool used is a familiar one. The ICO developed its security approach jointly with the NCSC precisely because data protection and cyber security are the same problem seen from two angles — get one wrong and the other is usually wrong too.
questions.reference: ICO Guide to Data Security

questions.scenario: A staff member reports that a laptop containing an unencrypted customer database was stolen from their car three days ago. Nobody has told the ICO yet, because “we're not sure if it counts as serious.”
questions.question: What does the UK GDPR require here?
options: Wait until you're completely certain before doing anything
Notify the ICO within 72 hours of becoming aware of the breach, where feasible — and inform affected individuals too if their rights and freedoms are at high risk
Only report it once the police confirm the laptop is unrecoverable
No obligation exists unless the data was specifically targeted by the thief
questions.explanation: Certain personal data breaches must be reported to the ICO within 72 hours of becoming aware of them, where feasible, and affected individuals must be informed without undue delay if there's a high risk to their rights and freedoms. Every breach — reportable or not — must also be logged internally.
questions.why: The 72-hour clock starts the moment you become aware, not once an investigation is finished — deliberately so, because delay is exactly what makes breaches worse for the people affected (stolen data tends to get used faster than most organisations can fully assess what happened). An unencrypted database on a stolen laptop is precisely the scenario breach-notification law was built around.
questions.reference: ICO Guide to Personal Data Breaches

questions.scenario: A former employee emails asking for a copy of all the personal data the company holds about them. The HR manager replies asking for a £10 fee before they'll start looking.
questions.question: Is charging a fee here compliant?
options: Yes — a reasonable admin fee is always allowed
No — in most circumstances you cannot charge a fee for a subject access request, and you must respond within one month
Yes, but only because they're a former rather than current employee
Only an issue if the request wasn't made in writing
questions.explanation: People have the right to access their personal data (a subject access request). In most circumstances no fee can be charged, and organisations must respond without undue delay and within one month of receipt — a request can be made verbally, in writing, or even via social media.
questions.why: The right of access exists so people can actually check what's being held and said about them — charging a fee before you'll even start looking creates exactly the barrier this right was designed to remove, which is why it's the exception rather than the norm (reserved for manifestly unfounded or excessive requests, or extra copies). The one-month clock doesn't pause just because the person has since left the organisation.
questions.reference: ICO Guide to Subject Access

questions.scenario: A customer asks a company to delete all their data. The company ignores the request for four months, because “we've been busy,” then confirms the data has now been removed.
questions.question: Does this meet the right to erasure requirements?
options: Yes, as long as the data was eventually deleted
No — organisations have one month to respond to an erasure request, and need a process to recognise, assess and act on it without undue delay
Yes — being busy is a recognised valid reason for delay
The right to erasure doesn't have a time limit
questions.explanation: The right to erasure (“the right to be forgotten”) gives individuals the right to have personal data erased in certain circumstances. Requests can be made verbally or in writing, and organisations have one month to respond — the right isn't absolute, but a valid request still needs a timely answer, not silence.
questions.why: A right that takes four months to even acknowledge isn't functioning as a right — the one-month timeframe exists so “erasure” means something close to immediate, not eventual. It's also not automatically granted just because someone asks: an organisation needs to actually check whether an exemption applies (a legal duty to retain the data, for example) rather than either ignoring the request or deleting on autopilot.
questions.reference: ICO Guidance on the Right to Erasure

questions.scenario: A company hires an external payroll bureau to run its monthly payroll. The bureau only acts on the company's instructions and doesn't decide what the data is used for or why.
questions.question: Under UK GDPR, what is the payroll bureau in this relationship?
options: The controller, since it physically handles the data
A processor — the organisation that decides the purposes and means of processing is the controller, regardless of what a contract calls anyone
A joint controller automatically, since it manages payroll
Neither term applies to payroll bureaus specifically
questions.explanation: Whether an organisation is a controller or processor depends on who determines the purposes and means of processing — not how a contract labels them. An organisation that only acts on another's instructions, without deciding why or how data is used, is a processor.
questions.why: This distinction isn't just semantics — the two roles carry genuinely different legal obligations, and getting it wrong (or leaving it undocumented) leaves both organisations exposed, since the ICO can act against controllers and processors alike, and individuals can claim compensation from either. It's worth actually documenting who is which for every organisation data gets shared with, rather than assuming a contract's wording has already settled it.
questions.reference: ICO Guide to Controllers and Processors

questions.scenario: A company starts recording employees' religion on its HR system “to plan diversity events better,” relying on the same general lawful basis (legitimate interests) it already uses for standard HR records, with no further checks.
questions.question: Is this sufficient to process this data lawfully?
options: Yes — one lawful basis covers all types of personal data equally
No — special category data like religion needs both a lawful basis under Article 6 and a separate condition for processing under Article 9; these aren't automatically the same thing
Yes, as long as employees aren't told which lawful basis is being used
Only relevant if the data is later shared outside the organisation
questions.explanation: Special category data needs more protection because it's sensitive. To process it lawfully you need both an Article 6 lawful basis and a separate Article 9 condition for processing — the two don't have to be linked, but both are required, and should be documented before processing begins.
questions.why: Article 9 exists because certain categories of data — health, religion, sexuality, ethnicity and others — carry a much higher risk of real harm if mishandled or exposed, so the law deliberately sets a higher bar than “we already had a general reason to hold HR data.” Skipping the extra check is a genuinely common mistake, precisely because it's easy to assume one lawful basis quietly covers everything a system happens to store.
questions.reference: ICO Guidance on Special Category Data
